title: Attend Every Meeting
statement:
You get a person's meetings for one day, meetings[i] = [start, end] with start < end, in no particular order. Return true if one person can attend all of them, and false if any two overlap.

Meetings are half-open: a meeting runs from start up to, but not including, end. So [1, 5] and [5, 8] do not overlap: you can leave one at 5 and walk into the next.

examples.why: [9, 11] and [10, 12] overlap. They are not next to each other in the list, so checking neighbours in input order misses it.
Sorted, the meetings are [1, 4], [4, 6], [6, 9]. Each ends exactly when the next begins, which is allowed.
An empty day has nothing to clash.

hints: Checking every pair works but is O(n²). Which meetings are the only ones that could clash with a given meeting, if the list were in a helpful order?
After sorting by start, a meeting can only clash with the one right before it, or an earlier one would also clash with that one.
Sort by start, then check each neighbouring pair: if a meeting starts before the previous one ends, return false.

explain.intuition:
If one person can attend everything, the meetings form a single line in time: each one ends before or exactly when the next one starts. So sort by start and look only at neighbours. If meeting B starts before the previous meeting A has ended, they clash. If no neighbouring pair clashes, no pair at all does, because every earlier meeting ended even before A did.

The boundary matters. Meetings are half-open, like a CSS animation that ends at 5 s while the next starts at 5 s: they do not overlap. So the clash test is start < previousEnd, strictly less.
pitfalls: Comparing neighbours without sorting first. Example 1 has its clashing pair at positions 0 and 2.
Using ≤ in the clash test. Back-to-back meetings like example 2 are fine.
Sorting the caller's array in place when the input should stay untouched. Copy first if that matters.

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: Two half-open meetings overlap when each starts before the other ends. Test all pairs.

solutions.title: Sort by start, compare neighbours
solutions.idea: In start order, a clash always shows up between two neighbours.

followups: If the answer is false, how many rooms would the meetings need? (That is the next problem.)
Meetings arrive one at a time and each must be accepted or rejected at once. What structure lets you check a new meeting in O(log n)?
